summary:
Sol Rewind is a free browser game for kids aged 7 to 12 that trains young players to run a small base on the Moon and then on Mars. Each day the player picks tasks at stations (water, power, radiation shield, experiments, rest, repairs), plays a short mini game for each task, and watches power, water and science change on a timeline. A day went badly? The player can rewind it and play it again, and everything comes back, except radiation. Radiation never goes back, just like in real space, so protecting the crew becomes the heart of the puzzle.

The game uses real NASA data: real solar storms from NASA DONKI decide the storm days, and real dose rates from NASA OSDR RadLab set the radiation scale. The 12 missions take place at real places, five Apollo landing sites and seven Mars missions, each with a real NASA photo. The Moon is the training ground where kids learn every system, and Mars is the harder test.

It matters because children learn how real missions are planned (power budgeting, life support, radiation safety, systems thinking, crew care and adapting to change) by playing, and they learn that a good space mission is about careful planning, not luck.
details:
What it does. Sol Rewind is a puzzle game about running a small outpost. A mission lasts 3 to 4 days. Each day the player chooses up to two to four tasks at the base (the number grows with the mission). Every task opens its own mini game, and how well the child plays decides how much water, power, protection or science the base gets. The base has water, power and astronaut energy, and the crew collects a radiation dose. To finish, the player must reach a science goal without running out of power or water, and with 3 stars also keep radiation low.

The core idea: rewind, but radiation stays. A timeline shows how each day went (a face for good, okay or rough), a graph of power, water and science, and a radiation row that only grows. Tapping a finished day lets the child replay from there. Power, water and science are restored, but the radiation already received stays with the crew. A faint "ghost" of the previous try shows what changed. This turns radiation safety into a planning problem: shield before the storm, not after.

How it works. The rules are a small set of pure functions (a simulation of days, tasks, costs, storms and failures), so replays are exact. Levels are data (JSON). Eight mini games share one contract and take a difficulty value, so later missions give more to do, not only more speed. Difficulty was tuned with a simple model of a young player and with a sampling solver that checks every level can be finished.

Real NASA data. Solar storms: real events from NASA DONKI (coronal mass ejections and their analyses, solar energetic particle events, geomagnetic storms), downloaded through the NASA Open APIs. Storm strength comes from the measured CME speed. Replays can draw other real storms of the same strength. Radiation: real dose rates from NASA OSDR RadLab for the ISS, lunar orbit and the surface of Mars during the May 2024 solar storm. Places: each of the 12 missions is set at a real site (Apollo 11, 12, 15, 16, 17; Viking 1, Opportunity, Spirit, InSight, Curiosity, Mars Pathfinder, Perseverance) with a real photo from the NASA Image and Video Library and coordinates from NASA NSSDCA. Companions: two real rovers teach facts, the Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle on the Moon and the Curiosity rover on Mars. Research links: NASA OSDR studies on astronaut health appear in the "In real life" cards. Every source is listed in the game's Sources and credits screen and in the repository (DATA_SOURCES.md, PHOTOS.md).

Benefits. Kids practice planning, budgeting and risk thinking in a friendly way and meet real space facts. There are no accounts, no tracking and no ads. It works on phones and computers, with large touch targets, picture-first cards, an optional read-aloud voice and a "How to play" story. Children can earn a postcard with the real photo of the place, a printable certificate, helmet colors and mission badges.

What we hope to achieve. A trainer that a child can start in seconds and that leaves them with one true idea they will remember: in space, some things you can undo and some things you cannot, so you plan ahead.

Tools and technology. TypeScript, Vite, GSAP (animation), SVG art drawn in code, Web Audio API (original music and sounds, no audio files), Web Speech API (read aloud), d3-geo and Natural Earth data (real continents), Tabler Icons, Vitest (76 automated tests). Hosted on GitHub Pages. Progress is saved only in the browser.

Play: https://shirkleyman.github.io/sol-rewind/ (add ?unlock to open every level). Code: https://github.com/shirkleyman/sol-rewind (Apache-2.0).
dataRefs: NASA DONKI space weather database (CME, CME Analysis, SEP, GST)
NASA OSDR RadLab radiation dose data (ISS, lunar orbit, Mars surface)
NASA Image and Video Library (photos of the 12 mission places and rovers)
NASA NSSDCA Apollo landing site coordinates
NASA Open Science Data Repository (OSDR) studies on astronaut health
projectRefs: Canadian Space Agency: Food production on the Moon and in remote areas (background)
ESA: communication beyond low Earth orbit (radio delay fact)
Natural Earth coastlines (public domain) via world-atlas
Open-source tools: Vite, Vitest, TypeScript, d3-geo, topojson-client (full list in NOTICE)
